analysis.one_liner: Overrides state right-to-work laws so unions can require workers to pay dues as a condition of employment.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal labor law, states may pass 'right-to-work' laws that bar union contracts from requiring workers to join or pay dues to the union that represents them. This bill repeals the federal provision that allows those state laws, which would let unions and employers negotiate contracts requiring union membership or fee payment anywhere in the country.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want union representation, and unions themselves. Repealing the state-law carve-out would allow union security clauses, which typically increase union membership and dues revenue, and stronger membership is generally associated with better pay and working conditions for represented workers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that lets states enact laws prohibiting agreements requiring union membership as a condition of employment [S2][S3].
With that provision gone, union contracts could include union security clauses regardless of state law, a change unions say would strengthen their membership base and bargaining position [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who do not want to join or financially support a union would lose the protection of state right-to-work laws and could be required to pay dues or fees to keep a job in a unionized workplace. Employers that rely on a nonunion or open-shop workforce would face stronger unions.

drawbacks.text: The core objection: the bill would allow contracts requiring workers to pay a union to keep their job, even if they disagree with the union, reversing the choice the roughly half of states made when they passed right-to-work laws (general knowledge about how section 14(b) works) [S2][S3].

Because workers in union workplaces are covered by the union's contract whether or not they join, supporters of right-to-work laws argue that requiring fees from dissenting workers infringes on individual choice; the bill removes states' authority to make that call for their own workers (general knowledge about exclusive representation) [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want collective bargaining, this would remove a major legal obstacle unions blame for weak membership in right-to-work states, and stronger unions historically correlate with higher wages for their members. The cost falls on workers who prefer not to fund a union and on employers who prefer a nonunion workforce, and it overrides state-level policy choices made through each state's own political process. The bill is a clean repeal with no compromise language, which is part of why it drew no Republican support.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on September 5, 2023, joined by 17 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that was the bill's last recorded action [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who prefer a nonunion workforce and benefit from state right-to-work laws are better off, since union security agreements remain banned in the states that prohibit them; unions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers opposed to union security agreements

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the federal provision allowing state right-to-work laws.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: 49 Senate Republicans, none of whom cosponsored
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the party has consistently supported state right-to-work laws.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents, including 16 of 48 Senate Democrats; not a single Senate Republican signed on, and no committee or floor vote ever tested the bill's support.

industries.note: The bill would let union contracts require membership or fee payment, boosting membership and dues. Stronger unions generally translate into higher pay and better conditions for the workers they represent.

Employers in right-to-work states would lose the guaranteed open-shop environment those laws provide and would face unions with stronger ability to require dues and organize. Their interest in keeping unions weak runs against workers seeking higher wages through bargaining.
